title: Todoist API: Authentication, Limits and Access (2026)
summary: Todoist API lets you read and write tasks and projects using personal tokens or OAuth. Confirm API availability for your subscription plan.
body_markdown:
## Calling Todoist Without Code Through Activepieces


You can make the same Todoist calls from a visual flow in Activepieces, where Todoist is one of 750 integrations counted from an open source monorepo with an MIT-licensed core, letting you combine multiple services in a single automation platform, so the tools you use are likely among the 750.


The wrapper above becomes a flow you build on a canvas and watch run, instead of a script you maintain.


The bootstrap version costs you an afternoon and no code, and flows are unlimited on every plan, free included; the self-hosted route is there if you'd rather not pay for a hosted plan.


### Connect Todoist without storing secrets


Add a Todoist step, choose to create a connection, and authorize your account when Todoist asks. You never paste a token into a script or store it in an environment file, so there's no secret sitting in a repository for a contractor to find.


Save the connection once and every flow in the project reuses it. That matters when you rotate access: you re-authorize one connection instead of hunting through every script that called the API.


### Build a calendar-event-to-task workflow


You build the flow in three parts, in this order:


1. Add a trigger for a new event in your calendar app, such as Google Calendar's new-event trigger, and load sample data so you can see the real fields.
2. Add the Todoist Create Task action and select your connection.
3. Map the fields: the event title into the task content, the event start into the due date, and the event description into the task description. Pick the target project explicitly, or tasks land in your Inbox.


When you map from sample data, you pick fields from a real event rather than guessing their names. A typo in a hand-written payload fails silently or errors at runtime; here you select the field and see its value.


Look at the screenshot below for the same pattern on a different job.


It's an invoice-collection flow whose canvas stacks five steps, from a Google Sheets trigger down to a Router, with the first step's settings panel open, so you can see how the Google Sheets trigger is configured.


Read it for the layout: the trigger sits at the top and each action below it. The panel shows the connection, the sample-data loader and a warning that Google can delay triggers by a few minutes.


That delay is a reminder that polling triggers aren't instant, so don't promise yourself real-time task creation.


After you publish, every run leaves a trace you can open, so when a task fails to appear you see which step stopped and what Todoist returned, instead of adding logging after the fact.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties are among the companies that run Activepieces.


You can also skip the canvas: describe the Todoist-to-calendar flow in Activepieces' built-in chat and what it publishes is a live flow in your account, the same one a builder would have assembled by hand, calling the same task and project endpoints.


It runs under the same RBAC and audit logs as any other flow, and its run trace shows exactly what happened at each step, readable by anyone on the team without a certification.


### Syncing Todoist with Google Calendar and Outlook


Pick the lightest option that meets your need. Native calendar subscription is free: Google Calendar can subscribe to an Outlook calendar's published link, and the reverse works too.


The catch is that subscribed ICS feeds refresh on the provider's schedule, so changes can show up hours late, and they're usually read-only.


When you need faster or genuinely two-way sync, build a workflow: one flow triggers on a new Google event and creates it in Outlook, and a second does the reverse.


Store the source event's ID on the copy and check for it first, or each flow will re-copy the other's events in a loop.
